lead: AM demodulation turns the received radio-frequency waveform back into the message. A cheap envelope detector uses a diode and an RC filter to follow the positive peaks of AM. A coherent detector multiplies by a locally generated carrier and low-pass filters; it also works when no carrier is sent. Envelope detection is common in medium-wave AM broadcast and simple receivers. Coherent detection is used in DSB-SC, SSB and laboratory systems. The choice depends on cost, carrier availability and the need for synchronization.
prereq: You need: 2.1 AM for the envelope Ac[1 + m(t)], 2.2 coherent detection for multiplication and filtering, and Unit 1 for low-pass filters.

sections.h3: Envelope detector: diode and RC load

blocks.text: An AM wave with carrier amplitude A<sub>c</sub> and normalized message m(t) is s(t) = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m(t)] cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t), where |m(t)| ≤ 1 and f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in Hz. The envelope E(t) = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m(t)] is the slow outline of the carrier. The diode conducts on positive half-cycles and charges the capacitor toward the peak. Between peaks the capacitor discharges through R. When RC is much larger than the carrier period, the output stays near the peak and follows E(t). A DC block removes the average A<sub>c</sub> and leaves A<sub>c</sub>m(t), the audio. The figure shows the order: diode, RC filter, DC block.
s(t) = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m(t)] cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t),   E(t) = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m(t)]
blocks.where: s(t) is the AM voltage in V; A<sub>c</sub> is the unmodulated carrier amplitude in V; m(t) is the normalized message, |m(t)| ≤ 1; f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in Hz; E(t) is the envelope voltage in V.

items: The diode rectifies the AM wave and passes positive peaks.
The capacitor charges to the peak and discharges slowly through R.
The RC low-pass filter removes the carrier, leaving the envelope.
The DC block removes A<sub>c</sub> and leaves the audio A<sub>c</sub>m(t).

sections.h3: RC design: ripple and diagonal clipping

blocks.text: RC must satisfy two limits: 1/(2π f<sub>c</sub>) ≪ RC ≪ 1/(2π W), where f<sub>c</sub> is carrier frequency in Hz and W is the highest modulating frequency in Hz. For small carrier ripple the practical rule is stronger: RC ≫ 1/f<sub>c</sub>, the carrier period. If RC is too small, the output has carrier ripple at f<sub>c</sub>. The upper limit lets the output fall with the fastest envelope; if RC is too large, the output cannot follow a fast downward slope, so diagonal clipping appears. For f<sub>c</sub> = 100 kHz and W = 1 kHz, 1.59 µs ≪ RC ≪ 159.15 µs, and the carrier period is 1/f<sub>c</sub> = 10 µs. Choose RC = 100 µs: the capacitor falls to e<sup>−10/100</sup> ≈ 0.90 of the peak between carrier peaks, about 10 % ripple, and 100 µs is below 159.15 µs, so there is no diagonal clipping at m = 0.5. Overmodulation with m > 1 makes 1 + m(t) negative. The envelope no longer matches the message, and a simple diode detector distorts. A DC block is needed because the detected output contains A<sub>c</sub> as well as the audio.

blocks.where: f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in Hz; W is the highest modulating frequency in Hz; R is the load resistance in Ω; C is the filter capacitance in F; RC is the discharge time constant in s.

items: RC too small: carrier ripple remains at f<sub>c</sub>.
RC too large: diagonal clipping on fast downward envelope slopes.
m > 1: a simple envelope detector cannot recover the message without distortion.

blocks.text: A coherent detector multiplies the received AM by a local carrier cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t) and low-pass filters the product. With s(t) = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m(t)] cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t), s(t)cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t) = (A<sub>c</sub>/2)[1 + m(t)] + (A<sub>c</sub>/2)[1 + m(t)]cos(4π f<sub>c</sub> t). The low-pass filter removes the double-frequency term; the output is (A<sub>c</sub>/2)[1 + m(t)]. A DC block then leaves (A<sub>c</sub>/2)m(t). The local carrier must match frequency and phase. A phase error φ reduces amplitude by cos φ; a frequency error smears the message. Coherent detection costs an oscillator and synchronization. It is necessary for DSB-SC and SSB, where the carrier is suppressed and the envelope is not the message. Broadcast AM can use the cheaper envelope detector.
y(t) = LPF{s(t) cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t)} = (A<sub>c</sub>/2)[1 + m(t)]
blocks.where: y(t) is the low-pass filter output in V; LPF means low-pass filter; s(t) is the received AM voltage in V; f<sub>c</sub> is the local carrier frequency in Hz; A<sub>c</sub> is the carrier amplitude in V; m(t) is the normalized message.

examples.question: An AM wave s(t) = 10[1 + 0.5 cos(2π1000t)] cos(2π100000t) V is detected by an envelope detector. Find the envelope, the audio output after DC blocking, and a suitable RC range. Use the 100 µs design value.
steps: Compare with s(t) = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + m cos(2π f<sub>m</sub> t)]cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t): A<sub>c</sub> = 10 V, m = 0.5, f<sub>m</sub> = 1000 Hz, f<sub>c</sub> = 100000 Hz, W = 1000 Hz.
Envelope E(t) = 10[1 + 0.5 cos(2π1000t)] V. It ranges from 10(1 − 0.5) = 5 V to 10(1 + 0.5) = 15 V.
DC block removes average A<sub>c</sub> = 10 V. Audio v<sub>o</sub>(t) = 10 × 0.5 cos(2π1000t) = 5 cos(2π1000t) V.

RC limits: lower 1/(2π f<sub>c</sub>) = 1/(2π × 100000) = 1.59 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s = 1.59 µs. Upper 1/(2πW) = 1/(2π × 1000) = 1.59 × 10<sup>−4</sup> s = 159.15 µs. Carrier period 1/f<sub>c</sub> = 1/100000 = 10 µs; low ripple needs RC ≫ 10 µs. The design value RC = 100 µs satisfies 1.59 µs ≪ 100 µs ≪ 159.15 µs and gives e<sup>−10/100</sup> ≈ 0.90 of the peak between carrier peaks.
examples.answer: E(t) = 10[1 + 0.5 cos(2π1000t)] V, audio v<sub>o</sub>(t) = 5 cos(2π1000t) V, and RC = 100 µs lies in the range 1.59 µs ≪ RC ≪ 159.15 µs.

m = 0.5
fm = 1000.0

traps: An envelope detector needs a carrier. Do not use it directly on DSB-SC or SSB, where the carrier is suppressed and the envelope is not the message.
RC too small gives carrier ripple at f<sub>c</sub>; RC too large gives diagonal clipping on fast envelope falls. Do not swap these.
Overmodulation with m > 1 makes the envelope cross zero; a simple diode detector distorts and a larger RC does not fix it.
The coherent output is (A<sub>c</sub>/2)[1 + m(t)] when the local carrier has unit amplitude. After a DC block, remove A<sub>c</sub>/2, not A<sub>c</sub>.
Use Hz for f<sub>c</sub> and W before computing RC. Mixing kHz and Hz is a common unit slip.

quiz.q: Which two main blocks form an envelope detector?
quiz.a: A diode and an RC low-pass filter, followed by a DC block in a receiver.

quiz.q: Why must RC be much larger than 1/(2π f<sub>c</sub>)?
quiz.a: It keeps the capacitor charged between carrier peaks, so the output follows the envelope and carrier ripple is small.

quiz.q: An AM wave is 8[1 + 0.4 cos(2π2000t)]cos(2π200000t) V. Find the audio after DC blocking.
quiz.a: A<sub>c</sub> = 8 V, m = 0.4. After DC blocking, v<sub>o</sub>(t) = 8 × 0.4 cos(2π2000t) = 3.2 cos(2π2000t) V.

quiz.q: What happens if the RC time constant is too large? Which part of the envelope is affected?
quiz.a: The capacitor discharges too slowly, so the output cannot follow fast downward envelope slopes. This is diagonal clipping, and the recovered audio is distorted.

quiz.q: What frequency must the local carrier of a coherent AM detector have?
quiz.a: The local carrier must have the same frequency f<sub>c</sub> as the incoming carrier, with the correct phase.

quiz.q: Why does a coherent detector work for DSB-SC even though no carrier is transmitted?
quiz.a: Multiplication by the local carrier shifts the sidebands to baseband and to twice the carrier frequency. The low-pass filter removes the double-frequency term and recovers the message.

quiz.q: For an envelope detector, f<sub>c</sub> = 1 MHz and W = 5 kHz. Give the RC range.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical AM radios add automatic gain control after the detector, which is receiver design rather than detection theory (see 2.7). Digital signal processors implement envelope detection by taking the magnitude of the analytic signal, using the Hilbert transform from Unit 1. Synchronous detectors appear in software-defined radio, where a local oscillator is a numeric cosine. Search next for envelope detector diagonal clipping, coherent demodulator carrier recovery, and synchronous AM detection.
